docuLanguageResource.title: Keynote speech by Commissioner Albuquerque at the Training Day' of the 10th Anniversary of the ECB Simulation Conference for University Students
docuLanguageResource.subtitle: Training Day' of the 10th Anniversary ECB Simulation Conference for University Students
docuLanguageResource.htmlContent:
Good morning, everyone.

I am delighted to join you for the opening of the 10th ECB Simulation Conference.

Let me begin by congratulating the organisers on a decade of an initiative that gives young people a unique opportunity to step into the shoes of Europe's monetary policymakers.

Congratulations also to all of you selected to participate. Over the next four days, I encourage you to make the most of this experience: challenge assumptions, test your ideas, exchange perspectives and learn from one another.

Today, I want to talk about financial services, how they can help us achieve our ambitions, and what we are doing to ensure they better serve the needs of Europeans.

But I want to approach this from a perspective particularly relevant to you.

Your generation is engaging with financial services in ways that are very different from those of previous generations, and that brings both new opportunities and new challenges. I have kept this in mind when preparing my remarks, and I look forward to hearing your own perspectives during our discussion.

 Over the past two decades, digital technology has transformed the way we interact with financial services. Paying a bill, transferring money or checking our balance now takes just a few taps on a screen.

For most of you, this is simply how the world works. You belong to a generation that has grown up with information, knowledge and financial services at your fingertips.

This is a significant advantage as you navigate important life decisions, from starting a career and buying a home to investing and preparing for retirement.

And many young Europeans are already actively investing. According to recent data from the European Securities and Markets Authority - ESMA -, 70% of new investors in 2025 were under 40, and a quarter were under 25.

We are also seeing a shift in investment preferences. ESMA's data show that, in 2025, over a third of equity investments made by adults aged 18 to 39 went into AI-related companies.

This curiosity and willingness to invest are real strengths. But regardless of our age or experience, we all need to understand the products we invest in, the costs involved and the risks we take.

Having access to more information does not necessarily mean being better informed. Not all information is reliable, not all products are suitable, and not all those offering financial guidance online are trustworthy.

The reality is that many of you learned like previous generations – through trial and error, rather than through structured educational programmes.

At the European Commission, we believe that such a structured education is something we should be providing to all Europeans - every generation at every stage in life.

To that end, last year we designed the first European Financial Literacy Strategy to bring those learnings to as many citizens as possible.  

And we don't need to start from scratch. There are many interesting and successful financial literacy initiatives already currently in action across the EU.

The intention with our strategy is to amplify these initiatives, see what has worked well, and bring those benefits across borders.

Just last week, at our high-level conference on financial literacy in Brussels we showcased some inspiring examples.

We had a project aimed at young students in Finland following a similar template to the one you are following this week. It focuses on real world experiences by running a fictional town and facing real-life financial decisions.

We also learned from an Irish initiative, FLiT,  which engages with women directly in their communities, helping them navigate financial challenges at different stages of their lives and giving them the knowledge and confidence to build long-term financial security.We showcased a Portuguese initiative that is developing a tool backed by AI that intends to protect citizens against financial fraud and scams, including by feeding the authorities with information that allows to identify almost instantly broad online fraud campaigns.

Good ideas should not be confined by national borders. Through our Financial Literacy Strategy, we want to help successful initiatives reach more people across Europe.

Last year we also issued Recommendations to Member States to make investing more accessible to Europeans through Savings and Investment Accounts and by developing supplementary pensions.

We have seen successful examples of Savings and Investment Accounts both in Europe and globally. We want Member States to build on these experiences, offering accounts that are easy to use, transparent, tax advantaged, giving Europeans more opportunities to make the most of their savings.

Because investing should not be a privilege reserved for the few. It should be an opportunity available to everyone, regardless of their financial background or the amount they can afford to save.

Let me give you an example of why investing, and with a long-term perspective, matters. According to European Commission calculations, between 2009 and 2024 – 15 years -, an investment tracking a broad European equity index would have gained more than 50% in purchasing power. Over the same period, money held in bank deposits would have lost more than 10% of its purchasing power, due to inflation.

Of course, past performance is no guarantee of future returns, and keeping some savings readily available is essential. But these figures illustrate the potential of long-term, diversified investment to grow our savings and help us achieve our goals.

And for your generation, there is one particularly valuable advantage: time.

Starting early, even with small amounts, allows investments more time to grow and gives you a longer horizon over which to navigate market fluctuations.

Let me now turn briefly to supplementary pensions.

Retirement may feel a long way off when you are at university.

But as people live longer, building additional retirement income alongside public pensions is becoming increasingly important. And here, too, starting early can make a significant difference.

Through our Recommendation, we want to raise awareness and make retirement saving easier, with clearer information, better tools to track pension entitlements and measures such as automatic enrolment.

The benefits go beyond individual savers. Long-term savings can also deepen Europe's capital markets and help finance innovative companies in strategic sectors, from artificial intelligence and quantum technologies to space, defence or the clean transition.

Europeans must always remain free to decide where and how to invest their money. Our responsibility is to ensure that those who choose to invest can do so easily, transparently and with confidence.

But making it easier for Europeans to invest is only one side of the equation. We also need to ensure that they have access to the opportunities offered by a truly integrated European capital market.

Today, Europe has people willing to invest and businesses looking for funding. Yet national barriers too often prevent them from connecting. Addressing this fragmentation is at the heart of our Market Integration and Supervision Package, presented last December.

By breaking down these barriers, we want to give investors greater choice and more opportunities to diversify, while enabling companies to access funding from across Europe.

Ultimately, this is about making our capital markets work better for citizens and businesses, while strengthening Europe's capacity to innovate, grow and compete globally.

Today, I have spoken about financial knowledge, access to trustworthy financial products, the importance of long-term investment and the opportunities that a more integrated European capital market can create.

But ultimately, our ambition is to build a Europe where your generation, and those that follow, have greater opportunities to achieve financial independence, build wealth and shape their own future.

And we cannot deliver on that ambition without listening to you, understanding your expectations and learning from your experiences.

Where do you turn to for financial information you can trust? What would encourage you to invest for the long term? What safeguards do you expect as financial services become increasingly digital?

You are not just the future users of Europe's financial system. You will also help shape it. And that is why your perspectives matter.

I very much look forward to hearing your ideas, your questions and, equally importantly, your challenges to what I have shared with you today.

Thank you.
